title: Psychological factors and indirect associations between depression and suicide risk in university healthcare students
abstract: Abstract Background Suicide risk is a major public health concern among university healthcare students. Although depression, hopelessness, experiential avoidance, and psychological well-being have each been associated with suicidal behavior, their simultaneous contribution to suicide risk and the indirect statistical associations among these variables remain insufficiently understood. Methods A total of 319 university healthcare students completed the Plutchik Suicide Risk Scale, the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II, the Beck Hopelessness Scale, the Depression subscale of the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) and the Psychological Well-being Scale for Adults. Sequential logistic regression models were used to examine factors associated with suicide risk, and a parallel multiple mediation analysis was performed to assess the indirect statistical associations between depression and suicide risk through hopelessness, experiential avoidance, and psychological well-being. Results Depression [OR = 1.117 (CI 95%: 1.050–1.190)], and hopelessness [OR = 1.395 (CI 95%: 1.209–1.624)] were significantly associated with suicide risk ( p < 0.001). No other variable was significantly associated with suicide risk ( p > 0.05). In the parallel multiple mediation analysis, a significant direct statistical association between depression and suicide risk was observed [b = 0.0955 (95% CI: 0.0365–0.1545), p < 0.01]. Among the indirect associations, only the statistical pathway through hopelessness was significant [b = 0.0673 (95% CI: 0.0385–0.1046)]. Conclusions In university healthcare students, depression and hopelessness are significantly associated with suicide risk.
